title: Systematic review of untreated remission from alcohol problems: Estimation lies in the eye of the beholder

claims.statement: In people with alcohol or drug problems followed for between about a year and several decades, a large share no longer met the criteria for a problem at a later interview, many of them without treatment, but how many depends on who was counted (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, or people who had already recovered), on how a problem, recovery ('remission') and treatment were defined, and on the length of the time window. Of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 US Army enlisted men who returned from Vietnam in September 1971 (interviews 8 to 12 months after return), 43% had used narcotics there (about a third of the men had tried heroin) and 20% reported having been dependent on narcotics there (21% by the study's own criteria for dependence), against 10% who had used narcotics and 0.7% who reported dependence (1% by the criteria) since their return; of 134 men from the study's two samples who were still dependent when they left Vietnam, 50% used narcotics again after return and 14% were dependent again (the two samples combined without weighting). The authors give a remission rate of 95% without saying which sample it describes; their figure, read approximately, shows that of the men first dependent in Vietnam, about 2% of 90 in the general sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample (selected on a urine test at departure positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) were dependent again. Remission there meant not being dependent again within about a year, many of the men counted as remitted still used narcotics, whether any had treatment is not reported, and the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change from Vietnam to home explains it (Robins et al., 1975). In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again about three years later (34,653 re-interviewed), 422 of the 1,172 people who met the criteria for alcohol dependence in the year before the first interview met them again in the year before the second (36%), so about 64% no longer met the full criteria (editors' calculation from unweighted counts), with persistence of 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52; no longer meeting the full criteria can include people with one or two symptoms left, and treatment between the interviews is not reported (Vergés et al., 2012). In 21 cohorts of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, 15 of them recruited through treatment, followed for 3 to 50 years (mean 17), published 2000–2015 and mostly from the US, 54% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of the people followed to the end were in remission at the last follow-up, and 35% (25% to 46%) of everyone enrolled when deaths and people lost to follow-up were counted as not remitted; single cohorts ranged from about 20% to 96%, remission was higher in cohorts followed longer, and the 6 cohorts not in treatment at the start did not differ detectably from the treatment cohorts (62% against 51%, p 0.42). Treatment during follow-up was not analysed, the pooled figure mixes very different follow-up times and so describes no particular time point, and the review did not appraise its cohorts (Fleury et al., 2016). For alcohol problems, a review of 124 published estimates of recovery without treatment (27 studies, 1976–2018, 24 of them North American) found figures from 2.7% to 98.3%, largely because the studies counted different things: among people already recovered, the share never treated (78% in two Canadian population surveys); among people with an alcohol problem who stayed untreated, the share who recovered (in the US national survey of 2001–2002, 12.4% when recovery meant not drinking and 32.6% when moderate drinking also counted; in a Dutch survey, 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, against 40% of those whose disorder was moderate or severe; in one US cohort of people initially without treatment, 36.0% fell to 14.0% when recovery also had to hold 16 years later); and among everyone with an alcohol problem, the share who recovered without treatment, which gave the lowest figures (2.7% to 63.6% in the nine studies that allowed all three counts). Most estimates covered about one year, the review did not appraise the studies, and these figures are second-hand (Mellor et al., 2019). So a high share of never-treated people among those who recovered and a much lower share of everyone with a problem recovering without treatment in a year can both be right. No source read here measured recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol; for the Vietnam veterans, treatment was not reported. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Robins et al. (1975), general sample N=451, before / in / since Vietnam: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; dependence self-reported 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%. Still dependent at departure (both samples, unweighted, n=134): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% dependent again. Men first dependent in Vietnam dependent again 8–10 months after return (Figure, approximate): about 2% (general sample, N=90) and about 7% (urine-positive sample, N=341). Stated remission rate 95% (no denominator). Vergés et al. (2012), NESARC 2001–2002 to 2004–2005: 422 of 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence (36%) dependent again about three years later, about 64% not (editors' calculation, unweighted); persistence 32.4% (ages 21–23) and 44.5% (43–52). Fleury et al. (2016), 21 cohorts, follow-up 3–50 years: standard remission 54.4% (95% CI 42.1–66.2), cohorts 19.6–95.7%, I² 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2–46.4), I² 99.5%; treatment at baseline 51.1% vs not 62.4% (p 0.421); longer follow-up, higher standard rate (B 0.046 per year, p 0.004). Mellor et al. (2019), alcohol, 124 estimates: 2.7% to 98.3%; nine studies with all three methods: all people with a problem 2.7–63.6%, untreated people 6.5–77.9%, remitted people 4.3–94.2% (unweighted medians 12.4, 38.9 and 43.9, not rates); 78% of remitted people untreated (two Canadian surveys); 12.4% vs 32.6% of untreated people remitted (abstinence vs abstinence or moderate drinking; NESARC); 78% vs 40% of people untreated for three years in remission (any vs moderate or severe disorder; Netherlands); 36.0% vs 14.0% (remission once vs also at 16 years; a US cohort).
